Nil TimeController delegates to time.After/time.Now; controlled mode is opt-in.

checks.reason: With Config.TimeController/RandomController nil (the production default), r.timeAfter/r.timeNow delegate to time.After/time.Now and r.randomTimeout falls back to the original rand.Int63()%minVal staggering (util.go randomExtra), so existing exported API behavior, timing, and persistence semantics are unchanged. checks.name: message_cache_injection_coherence

evidence.reason: Sole consumer of the wrapped channel; forwards unchanged in pass-through and retains in controlled mode.
RespChan swap and separate response entries with reversed Source/Target and new handles.
Same-path delivery with entry-preserving classified errors and removal only on acceptance.

checks.reason: CapturingTransport.serve is the sole consumer of the wrapped transport Consumer channel, so no in-boundary message bypasses the controller. Capture deep-copies the command, buffers the snapshot stream, swaps RespChan to capture responses as separate reversed-routing entries, and Inject delivers the controller-private copy into the same normal ingress (consumerCh for requests, preserved RespChan for responses). Handles are monotonic unexported uint64, invalidated after Drop/Clear/successful Inject, and cache mutations are mutex-guarded.

checks.name: original_send_suppressed

evidence.reason: Controlled branch retains without forwarding; only pass-through branch forwards.

checks.reason: While capture is enabled, handleRPC calls MessageController.capture and does not forward the original RPC into the target consumer channel; the original sender remains blocked on its preserved response channel until the captured request and its response are injected. There is no path that both forwards and retains a message.

checks.name: protocol_logic_unchanged

evidence.reason: Returns true immediately when r.paused is false, making the added gates no-ops by default.
TimeController/RandomController wiring is conditional on non-nil config fields.

checks.reason: All production behavior is default-disabled: lifecyclePauseGate returns immediately when not paused, the pause fields are unused without a LifecycleController, and TimeController/RandomController hooks only activate when explicitly configured. Default message transport remains pass-through. No state-transition, persistence, ordering, or message semantics changed in default mode.

checks.name: testing_contract_conformance

evidence.reason: for i < steps { stepOnce() } with no inter-step processing boundary.
Only submits due timers; does not run protocol goroutines, so reactive re-arms are deferred past the whole Advance(n) call.
Crash = Shutdown; does not provide a crash-specific termination that tracks all execution contexts.
Started with plain 'go func()', not r.goFunc, so waitShutdown does not await it.
Untracked goroutine that may complete after Shutdown/Crash returns.

checks.reason: Two fixed guarantees are not met. (1) TimeController.Advance(steps) runs stepOnce in a tight loop without yielding to protocol goroutines, so timers re-armed by processing an earlier step are not registered before later stepOnce iterations; this makes Advance(n) observably different from n separate Advance(1) calls and can skip intermediate reactive re-arms. (2) LifecycleController.Crash is a facade over Raft.Shutdown, whose waitShutdown only waits for routinesGroup-tracked goroutines; the plain 'go' leadership-transfer goroutines are untracked and may still respond or mutate state after Crash returns.

issues.reason: Advance(steps) iterates stepOnce without allowing protocol goroutines to process submitted events between steps. A timer re-armed in reaction to step i's delivery is registered only after the whole Advance(n) call has already advanced the clock, so its deadline is computed against a later 'now'. For example, a follower with a 1-step heartbeat timer receives one delivery from Advance(2) instead of the two deliveries produced by two separate Advance(1) calls. This violates the fixed guarantee that Advance(n) is equivalent to n calls of Advance(1) including reactive timer re-arming.

Crash is implemented solely as Raft.Shutdown().Error(), and Raft.Shutdown's waitShutdown only waits for goroutines registered through raftState.goFunc. Leadership-transfer goroutines started with plain 'go' (raft.go:815 and raft.go:873) are not tracked, so they can call future.respond and setLeadershipTransferInProgress after Crash returns. This violates the requirement that after Crash returns no abandoned execution context may emit output or mutate protocol state; the crash path needs to track or terminate these contexts rather than labeling the operation a pure facade.

risks: Stop and Crash converge behaviorally in this target because Raft.Shutdown is documented as 'not a graceful operation', Raft persists term/vote/logs eagerly, and the WithClose transport close is cleanup rather than a persistence flush; the controller records stopped vs crashed phase, but the durable state recovered by Restart is identical.

Response watcher goroutines created per captured request live until the corresponding response arrives or the decorator closes, so a long-running controlled session that injects many requests without transport shutdown can accumulate goroutines (a resource cost, not a correctness violation).
